assessments.reasoning: The README sets the applicability boundary. It identifies Rocq as the prover and describes a language in which users can define mathematical objects, express executable algorithms, and state theorems. It leaves that language unnamed. The dependency applies as context only. I opened the retained original README and SSReflect reference and verified both full-body and passage digests against the same pinned repository revision.

The SSReflect reference identifies Gallina as the language Coq uses for logical specifications. It distinguishes the programming subset used in small-scale reflection from the additions SSReflect makes to Gallina. This supplies the name under the historical Coq wording. With the README's same-revision product context, the evidence sustains the two document attributions in the claim.

challenge.method: Read the introduction on its own and identify which entity receives a proper name. Check whether the naming phrase applies only to the programming subset or to an SSReflect extension, and whether the shared revision establishes equivalence across editions.
challenge.results: The introduction names the prover. Inferring Gallina's name from that passage alone would exceed its content. The separate SSReflect passage supplies the naming evidence. The naming phrase identifies Gallina itself. The passage separately describes a subset and extensions to the language. The joint reading links the discovery lead to Gallina at the pinned revision and supplies no basis for merging prover and language identities or inferring semantic continuity across releases.

limitations: The README names the prover. The same-commit SSReflect reference supplies the Gallina name, using the historical Coq wording.
The evidence links the discovery lead to the existing Gallina language identity. Prover identity, SSReflect extensions, and edition-to-edition semantics remain separate.
